whatItDoes: Finds the break-even point for a product or business: the number of units you must sell so that revenue exactly covers fixed costs plus variable costs. It also shows break-even revenue and the contribution margin per unit.
whyItExists: Launching a product or running a business without knowing the break-even point risks pricing that can never cover costs. The calculation separates what must be sold before profit exists, which anchors pricing, marketing, and budget decisions.
whoShouldUse: Founders pricing a product, small-business owners planning costs, and anyone evaluating a new offering's viability.
useCases: Decide if a selling price covers fixed and variable costs
Set a sales target before a product becomes profitable
See how a price change shifts the break-even point
Estimate how fixed-cost cuts reduce required volume
Evaluate whether a new product line is worth launching
Budget marketing spend against the volume it must generate
instructions: Enter total fixed costs for the period
Enter the selling price per unit
Read the units and revenue needed to break even
Adjust price or costs to see how the point moves
Use the contribution margin to reason about volume targets
examples: $50,000 fixed, $15 variable, $45 price → 1,667 units — a $5 price rise cuts required volume by 17%
$30,000 fixed, $10 variable, $25 price → 2,000 units with a $15 contribution margin per unit
bestPractices: Be honest about all fixed costs, from rent to software
Update variable costs whenever suppliers or labor change
Use break-even as a floor, not a target — profit needs more
Re-run the math if the price changes
Stress-test with a higher variable cost to build a safety margin
commonMistakes: Excluding fixed costs like rent, salaries, and tools
Pricing below variable cost, making break-even impossible
Treating break-even units as if profit comes automatically
Forgetting that break-even assumes every unit sells at the same price
Ignoring the cash-flow timing of when fixed costs actually come due
faq: Is this financial advice? — No, it is a planning estimate.
What if price is below variable cost? — Every sale loses money and there is no break-even point.
What is contribution margin? — Selling price minus variable cost; the amount each unit contributes to fixed costs and profit.
Is my data shared? — No, the calculation runs locally in your browser.
How do I profit above break-even? — Every unit sold past break-even adds the full contribution margin to profit.
Does break-even account for taxes? — No, it covers operating costs only; taxes are separate.
